knowledge_records.scenario: My vehicle has broken down while I am driving. What should I do immediately?
knowledge_records.answer: Do not brake abruptly. Take your foot off the accelerator and decelerate smoothly. Turn on your hazard warning lights immediately. Steer the vehicle towards the left side of the road, ideally onto the shoulder or emergency lane. Once stopped, apply the handbrake, turn the steering wheel away from the road, and turn off the engine.
key_actions: Turn on hazard warning lights immediately
Decelerate smoothly without sudden braking
Steer to the left shoulder or emergency lane
Apply the parking/hand brake
Turn the steering wheel away from the road
Turn off the engine
do_not: Do not make sudden maneuvers or abrupt braking
Do not stop in a live traffic lane if a shoulder is available
Do not leave the vehicle in gear without applying the handbrake
escalation_criteria: Vehicle stops in a live traffic lane with no safe path to the shoulder
Vehicle is struck by another vehicle while stopping
knowledge_records.notes: Based on standard highway safety protocols and Indian traffic rules requiring movement to the leftmost side during emergencies.

knowledge_records.scenario: My car has stopped on the side of the road. How do I warn other drivers?
knowledge_records.answer: Keep your hazard warning lights on at all times. If it is safe to exit the vehicle, place a reflective warning triangle at least 10 meters (or more on high-speed roads) behind your vehicle to warn approaching traffic. Indian law requires all motor vehicles to carry a reflective warning triangle.
key_actions: Keep hazard warning lights continuously on
Carefully exit the vehicle on the non-traffic side if safe
Place a reflective warning triangle at least 10 meters behind the vehicle
do_not: Do not exit the vehicle into the live traffic lane
Do not use flares or unsafe burning markers
Do not stand behind the vehicle while placing the triangle
escalation_criteria: Unable to deploy the triangle safely due to fast-moving traffic
knowledge_records.notes: Central Motor Vehicle Rules (CMVR) mandate the carrying of a reflective warning triangle (Rule 125-A).

knowledge_records.scenario: My vehicle has broken down on a national highway or expressway. What specific steps should I take?
knowledge_records.answer: Move to the extreme left shoulder or emergency lane immediately. Turn on hazard lights. If you are on a national highway, you can call the NHAI highway helpline at 1033 for emergency patrol assistance. Do not attempt to cross the highway on foot. Stay inside the vehicle with seatbelts fastened if the shoulder is narrow or traffic is very fast; otherwise, exit safely from the left side and stand behind the metal guardrail.
key_actions: Move to the left shoulder
Activate hazard lights
Call NHAI 1033 for national highway assistance
Remain inside with seatbelts on if the shoulder is narrow or unsafe to exit
If exiting, use the left door and stand behind the guardrail
do_not: Do not cross the highway on foot
Do not stand between your vehicle and passing traffic
Do not walk along the highway shoulder seeking help
escalation_criteria: Vehicle is stopped in a live high-speed lane
Another vehicle is approaching rapidly and cannot change lanes
knowledge_records.notes: NHAI operates the 1033 helpline for distressed commuters on national highways.

knowledge_records.topic: Stay inside vs. leave the vehicle
knowledge_records.scenario: After my car broke down on the highway, should I stay inside or get out?
knowledge_records.answer: The decision depends on the traffic and available safe space. If traffic is moving very fast, the shoulder is narrow, or there is no safe area behind a guardrail to stand, it is generally safer to stay inside the vehicle with seatbelts fastened and hazard lights on. If there is a wide shoulder and a safe area behind a guardrail or embankment, exit the vehicle from the side away from traffic (typically the left door in India) and wait there.
key_actions: Assess the speed of traffic and width of the shoulder
Stay inside with seatbelts on if the shoulder is narrow or there is no safe refuge
Exit via the non-traffic side door if a safe area behind a barrier exists
do_not: Do not stand directly in front of or behind the vehicle
Do not stand on the shoulder adjacent to live traffic without a barrier
escalation_criteria: Signs of fire or fuel leak (evacuate immediately regardless of traffic)
knowledge_records.notes: General roadside safety principle widely recognized by Indian highway authorities.

knowledge_records.topic: Mechanical warning signs requiring immediate stopping
knowledge_records.scenario: I am driving and my engine temperature gauge is in the red, or I smell fuel, or my brakes feel unresponsive. Should I keep driving to a mechanic?
knowledge_records.answer: No. If you experience severe overheating, brake failure, steering failure, strong fuel smell, or sudden heavy smoke, you must stop the vehicle immediately and safely. Continuing to drive can lead to a fire, complete loss of control, or a severe accident. Pull over to a safe spot, turn off the engine, and do not attempt to continue driving.
key_actions: Pull over and stop the vehicle immediately
Turn off the engine
Activate hazard lights
Exit the vehicle if there is smoke or fuel smell (cross-reference DOMAIN-006)
do_not: Do not keep driving in the hopes of reaching a mechanic
Do not open the radiator cap if the engine is overheating (severe burn risk)
Do not ignore warning lights on the dashboard
escalation_criteria: Smoke or strong fuel smell (Escalate to DOMAIN-006: Vehicle Fire)
knowledge_records.notes: Basic vehicle safety guidelines issued by transport authorities globally and within India.

knowledge_records.scenario: My car has broken down and I have passengers, including children. What should I do?
knowledge_records.answer: Ensure all passengers remain calm. If it is safe to exit (wide shoulder, barrier present), have all passengers exit from the doors away from traffic (typically left doors in India). Ensure they move immediately behind a guardrail or up an embankment. Never let passengers stand near the vehicle on the traffic side. If it is unsafe to exit, keep passengers inside with seatbelts fastened.
key_actions: Instruct passengers to remain calm
Exit from the non-traffic side doors only
Move passengers well away from the vehicle, behind a guardrail
Keep children under close supervision
do_not: Do not let passengers exit into the live traffic lane
Do not allow passengers to wait inside the vehicle if there is a fire or fuel smell hazard
Do not let children play near the roadside
escalation_criteria: Passengers are injured or the vehicle is in a dangerous position
knowledge_records.notes: Standard passenger safety protocol during roadside emergencies.

knowledge_records.scenario: My car broke down on a highway at night. What extra precautions should I take?
knowledge_records.answer: Visibility is severely reduced at night. Keep all hazard lights and parking lights on to make the vehicle visible to approaching traffic. If you have a flashlight, use it to warn oncoming traffic or to safely walk to place the reflective warning triangle further back (at least 50 meters on a highway). Do not stand on the road. Stay inside the vehicle if the shoulder is narrow, as other drivers may not see you standing on the side.
key_actions: Keep hazard and parking lights on
Deploy reflective warning triangle at a greater distance (e.g., 50+ meters)
Use a flashlight if available
Strongly prefer staying inside the vehicle unless a well-lit safe zone behind a barrier exists
do_not: Do not stand on the road or shoulder where drivers cannot see you
Do not use your phone screen as a light source while standing near traffic
escalation_criteria: Vehicle lights are completely non-functional due to electrical failure
knowledge_records.notes: Based on CMVR requirements for reflective triangles and general night-breakdown safety. Exact distances for triangle placement on varying Indian road types are not explicitly standardized for the public in one single document, hence Medium confidence on exact distance.

knowledge_records.scenario: My car has broken down and I see smoke coming from the engine or smell strong fuel. What should I do?
knowledge_records.answer: If you see smoke or smell fuel, treat this as a high-risk fire situation. Turn off the engine immediately. Evacuate all passengers from the vehicle quickly, moving away from the smoke and fuel smell. Do not open the hood if there is heavy smoke, as oxygen can feed a fire. Move to a safe distance away from traffic and the vehicle. This situation requires escalation to fire safety protocols.
key_actions: Turn off the engine immediately
Evacuate all occupants quickly
Do not open the hood if smoke is present
Move to a safe distance (at least 30 meters away)
Call emergency services (fire brigade)
do_not: Do not open the hood to inspect the engine if smoke is billowing
Do not attempt to retrieve belongings from the vehicle
Do not re-enter the vehicle
escalation_criteria: Visible flames (Escalate to DOMAIN-006: Vehicle Fire)
Strong fuel spill (Escalate to DOMAIN-006: Vehicle Fire)
knowledge_records.notes: Cross-domain escalation to DOMAIN-006. General safety principle for vehicle fire hazards.
